name: Occupancy rate
seoDesc: Occupancy rate: work out rooms occupied (in a day) from the rooms in maintenance/unavailable and the room-nights in maintenance. A free finance calculator…
summary: The Occupancy rate calculator turns the rooms in maintenance/unavailable, the room-nights in maintenance and the total rooms into rooms occupied (in a day). It is built for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the Occupancy rate calculator work?
sections.html:
The Occupancy rate calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports rooms occupied (in a day) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the period); then you type in the rooms in maintenance/unavailable, the room-nights in maintenance, the room-nights in maintenance (2) and the total rooms.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Occupancy rate calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Rooms occupied (in a day)=(1 ÷ 100) × daily rate × (-rooms in maintenance ÷ unavailable + total rooms)
Total rooms=(1 ÷ 30) × (room-nights in maintenance × monthly rate + 100 × room-nights (in a month)) ÷ monthly rate
Rooms-nights (custom time)=(1 ÷ 100) × custom rate × (calculate occupancy for × total rooms − room-nights in maintenance)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Time, opening in days
  • %, opening in percent
  • %, opening in percent
  • %, opening in percent

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Occupancy rate calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the rooms in maintenance/unavailable, the room-nights in maintenance and the total rooms — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Occupancy rate calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns rooms occupied (in a day), derived from the rooms in maintenance/unavailable, the room-nights in maintenance and the total rooms. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Occupancy rate calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the rooms in maintenance/unavailable, the room-nights in maintenance and the total rooms, which is 12 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter calculate occupancy for in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Calculate occupancy for opens in days and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Occupancy rate calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
